The question of whether online degrees are valued less by employers yields genuinely conflicting evidence across the retrieved sources. On one side, a 2023 GMAC Corporate Recruiter Survey found that only about half of global employers view online and in-person degrees equally, and nearly two-thirds believe in-person graduates have stronger leadership, communication, and technical skills [d1]; in the US specifically, only 27% of recruiters said their organizations value the two formats equally [d8]. Rigorous field experiments further show that applicants with degrees from for-profit online institutions were called back 22–25% less often than those from public universities for business positions requiring a bachelor's degree [d2][d10], with Brookings noting that "employers are still wary about the skills of those with online higher education credentials (at least those from for-profit institutions)" [d9]. On the other side, a CareerBuilder survey found that 83% of executives consider an online degree as credible as a campus-based one [d6], and the 2019 Trends in Online Education Report found only 10% of employers believe online learning is inferior to on-campus learning [d7]. Sources from Schiller University and Point Loma University argue that accredited online degrees are valued equally and that employers actually appreciate the self-discipline and time management skills online graduates demonstrate [d4][d5], while TheBestSchools.org states that "an online degree holds just as much weight as a traditional degree" [d3]. In summary, employer attitudes toward online degrees are not uniform: perceptions depend heavily on whether the institution is for-profit or nonprofit/accredited, the region, and the industry, with research experiments tending to show a penalty for for-profit online credentials while broader surveys suggest growing acceptance of accredited online programs.
